#1326. Kane’s record-equalling cap was no different to his first

The 125th cap was no different to the first for Harry Kane, who has now been in the business of goal accumulation for so long that it is only at the landmark moments, that all of us are obliged to step back and take in the full scale of the work he has created.

Peter Shilton took 20 years to rack up his 125 caps, while for Kane it has been just 11 – and then there are the goals. Two more on Tuesday took him to 91 which means that only 12 other England players in history have more England caps than Kane has England goals. This unassuming man from Chingford, who looks like a mildly rebellious academic from the late 1950s, was at it again: the first-time strike, the back-post header. He has some misses across these 11 years, most infamously from the penalty spot against France at the Qatar World Cup almost four years ago, so, yes, there are some regrets too. But what sticks is the way he has taken his chances – again and again.

ONE-TOUCH BRILLIANCE! ✨ Anderson, Rogers and Kane combine beautifully to double England's lead 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Cap No. 125, goal No. 90 for the skipper 👏 https://t.co/otMcxlXyps

Following his debut goal in 2015 against Lithuania, Kane has missed just 27 of the 152 England games since. He has added to the total like a great Test batsman patiently moving the scoreboard along. There was a bad run without goals in 2020 and before that in 2018. He scored only five in his first 17 caps and then scored 14 in his next 10. Against a very mediocre Czech Republic team this was classic late-era Kane, picking his moments and taking those chances with the usual absence of nerves. He was even substituted before the end.

Hall ➡️ Kane! The Newcastle fullback swings in the corner and it's the England captain who rises highest to head home 💥 https://t.co/5EhAcNZUqm

Afterwards at a Wembley press conference to mark the occasion, he invoked the cricket analogy himself on the question of scoring 100 England goals. “Being in the 90s, I try not to think about it too much, and it’s like I guess being a cricketer in the 90s. The more you think about the hundred… you don’t always get there.” There has still not been the elusive major trophy in the Kane England years but there has been success relative to the three decades that came before it. Semi-finals, finals – a good team if not a winning team.

At the centre of it has been a man around whom there has never been any scandal or, by the usual measure, much that might be described as spectacular. Rather it has been the scope of Kane’s career that is the most striking. The volume of the goals, of appearances, the capacity to be available – to play, to score – and the absolute quality of the player himself. He is determined to wring the very last drop out of his talent and usually refuses to acknowledge the prospect of the end, although there was a nod to it this time. “At some stage you know this opportunity isn’t going to be here,” he said. “I’m not going to be around forever, and I still hope that’s a long way away. But ultimately, of course, there’s times you’re tired or you’re injured, but I know I’ll miss it when it’s done. I try to always remind myself that and always try to make myself available.”

One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he said, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

England kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.

Thomas Tuchel believes England have taken a step forward from their World Cup heartbreak over this international break and said he was “honoured” to hear fans sing his name.

England finished their four Nations League games with a 3-0 win over Czech Republic, in which Harry Kane scored twice on his record-equalling 125th appearance.

It meant that Tuchel’s team have won three and lost one, against Spain, of their four games since the World Cup, after which the England head coach was heavily criticised for the semi-final defeat to Argentina.

Tuchel seems to have won the forgiveness of some England supporters, who sang his name at the start and the end of Tuesday’s game.

“It means a lot,” Tuchel said. “It’s amazing to have a song. It’s the biggest honour. And I’m very happy and very honoured. They can be sure that I will give my absolute best to make our team win and play well.”

Asked if he sensed a change in mood around his England team since the fall-out from the World Cup, Tuchel said: “I do and I think it’s necessary to move on. I think I can only repeat that we didn’t go out in the group stage. Sometimes it feels like that and we didn’t. As I said, our aim was always to progress, move forward and improve.”

Tuchel snapped back at a reporter who questioned why he felt it necessary to repeat that England had not gone out in the group stage of the World Cup, claiming the criticism had felt a “little bit” too harsh.

But on whether England have shown they are a step ahead of where the team were at the World Cup during this international camp, Tuchel was far more positive and replied: “Of course and that’s what we have to do. That is our goal to constantly improve and develop.

“We had these experiences together and we had a big tournament together, and it was very positive. It’s necessary to move forward and improve, especially in sports. This is what we’re trying to do.

“We adjusted some details in our structure and we didn’t compromise on the effort and the intensity, and on the togetherness of the team. The players who were with us in the World Cup took care of these standards and of the culture within the team, off the pitch and on the pitch, and I think that’s what you could see.”

We played a very good match, very fluid and to put it into context it was the fourth match in 11 or 12 days. We dominated the whole match, had some good opportunities, scored some beautiful goals. Subs were strong. Very good performance again.

[Leading the way, Mr Kane] Of course. That’s what he does. I don’t take it for granted. It’s just exceptional, every single match. It’s just difficult to find new words to express it.

Training, attitude, cohesion, belief, of course [is why they’re stronger than ever].

[Has the World Cup made England stronger?]  Of course, we got the first medal in 60 years. We didn’t go out in the group stage. We had a strong qualification, strong World Cup and strong camp. All four matches were on a high level. The camp throughout from the first day was on the highest level. You learn every day together. We grew stronger.

I was happy that everyone who was in the camp was contributing. Everyone was on the pitch. Everyone showed he was willing to give everything for the team and for the shirt. The guys who were with us for the World Cup set the standards high, made everyone feel welcome and everyone had a good camp.

He’s the best England player evert to wear the shirt and it’s an honour to play with him. And he’s only getting better.

A perfect night for me personally and also for the team. It’s been a tough camp, a long camp with some difficult games so it’s nice to finish it off all together. An extremely proud evening for me.

You saw some fantastic football out there tonight. The way we’re moving, the one-touch stuff, a fantastic ball from Elliot to Morgan and then a first time cross which was as good as it gets. As a striker you’re just waiting for those opportunities.

It started in the first game [reaching a higher level] although the result didn’t go for us. First game after a tournament, obviously this was a four-game camp, we had to find it [a higher level] and find it quickly. That’s the most pleasing thing.

This is the England team. There’s always going to be competition for places. It’s about taking the opportunity whether it’s 90 minutes, five minutes, whatever it was, make the most of it. You’re seeing that, everyone wants to be part of this. That’s only going to make us better for sure.

[Now for cap 126 next month?] That would be nice for sure.

Secret to Harry Kane’s England longevity? ‘He strikes the ball better than Ronaldo’

Right foot, goal. Left foot, goal. Edge of the area, goal. Inside the area, goal. Under pressure, goal, Right foot, save. Left foot, goal. That was Harry Kane’s warm-up prior to England’s 7-0 demolition of Croatia and it underlined just why the striker will equal Peter Shilton’s appearance record on Tuesday night.

As demonstrated in Rijeka, Kane’s career has been a non-stop pursuit of excellence that has led him to the very top of the national game. England’s record goalscorer will also become the joint most-capped player with Shilton, when he makes his 125th appearance against the Czech Republic at Wembley on Tuesday night.

Eberechi Eze is set to start for England in the clash against Czech Republic tonight. The Arsenal forward is poised to come in for Anthony Gordon, who has started in the three matches during the Nations League international break. Trent Alexander-Arnold is also due to play at right-back, with Jarell Quansah moving to centre-back to cover for Ezri Konsa.

Alex Scott has been ruled out through injury, which has upset Bournemouth after he played in the win over Croatia at the weekend. Myles Lewis-Skelly is expected to get a recall to the team after playing against Czech Republic in Prague last week when England won 2-0. Morgan Rogers, who scored against Croatia, is in line to start in place of Bukayo Saka.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of England vs Czech Republic from Wembley in the fourth and mercifully final round of fixtures in this sprawling Nations League international break. Tonight Harry Kane will win his 125th cap and equal Peter Shilton for England appearances.

Shilton’s took him 20 years as Gordon Banks was simply too good in the couple of years following his debut and then a couple of managers, Don Revie and Ron Greenwood, preferred Ray Clemence until the latter finally plumped for Shilton as No 1 in 1979. Kane’s, by contrast, have taken him 11. In that time he has been rested for a handful of friendlies but has not been unused in a competitive match when fit since Gareth Southgate left him out of the 5-0 victory over Sam Marino in 2021’s World Cup qualifier when Dominic Calvert-Lewin scored two and Ollie Watkins one goal on his debut.

England played the Czech Republic a week ago, winning 2-0 in Prague by virtue of Anthony Gordon’s cute header and Kane’s clever shot through a defender’s legs but they huffed and puffed for ages against a team harshly reduced to 10 men until they blew the house down. They went on to marmalise Croatia 7-0 in their next game in front of a crowd that sounded like a cross between the choirs on Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2 and There’s No One Quite Like Grandma.

In the past England have had problems backing up their best performances – the 4-1 evisceration of the Dutch at Euro 96 was followed by the cagey display in the quarter-final against Spain before prevailing on penalties, the 5-1 victory in Munich in 2001 led to a drab 2-0 win against Albania at St James’ Park the following Tuesday, in 2016 they went to Berlin and beat world champions Germany but were thumped by Netherlands, who had not even qualified for Euro 2016, a couple of days later. Even their thrilling, second-half showing against Croatia in their World Cup opener in June preceded the dreary 0-0 draw with Ghana.

Given the attacking fluency in Rijeka, Thomas Tuchel must be tempted not to to ring the changes and replace seven or eight players. He will have to find replacements for the injured Alex Scott and Ezri Konsa, however, and Calvert Lewin, who has had seven minutes of action, Rio Ngumoha 19, Morgan Gibbs-White 27 and Jarrad Branthwaite one, may feel they deserve a fairer opportunity to show what they can do in a match.

#1324. Kai Havertz leads the Premier League in offsides as Arsenal pile up infractions in 1-0 win over Hull City

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LONDON -- Though there was some to-ing and fro-ing as to the order in which the offenses should be considered, it seemed fitting that what would have been Arsenal's best scoring chance of the first half of their 1-0 win over Hull City was wiped out for an offside. Here is a team whose attack has been drifting so out of sync that promising situations fall apart without the opponent needing to get involved.

Sometimes the opponent is even willing to offer them a helping hand. Only the members of the International Football Association Board might be able to say for sure whether Arsenal should have had a penalty when Kai Havertz's shirt was pulled by Hull City's Nobel Mendy as Bruno Guimaraes took a long-range shot. The striker was impeded, but he had been standing in an offside area. Was he attempting to play the ball when Mendy grabbed hold of his jersey? If not, then the foul should have taken precedence and Arsenal should have had a penalty. Instead, they had to wait until the 72nd minute for their win, Martin Odegaard bundling in the rebound off Noni Madueke's shot.

At least that meant Mikel Arteta could jokingly say he had not seen the spot kick that might have been. There may be a question about that particular penalty and offside, but the big-picture statistics are mind-boggling, such that there surely has to be some air in these numbers.

In the last seven Premier League seasons, no team has averaged more than three offsides per game. Only Burnley in 2021-22 and Liverpool two years later have averaged more than 2.5, in the process reaching over 100 for the season. In their 10th game of the season, Arsenal committed offside offenses Nos. 32, 33, 34 and 35. At the final whistle, that was 11 more than any other team in the league, and there is a very real prospect that lead does not get eaten into. Field a team of Pippo Inzaghis and you'd do well to put up these numbers.

There has to be something to this, right?

What makes this all the more curious is that Arsenal have not been a team that particularly struggled to stay onside before this season. In the previous six campaigns, they were caught about as often as the average Premier League team when you adjust for possession. When these relatively low-volume statistics warp like this, at least part of the answer is going to be variance. A bit more of it might be that Arsenal have a 10-game sample size that includes Aston Villa. Still, that sample is over a quarter of the season. Arsenal have had a string of games where they have been caught offside with frequency.

This looks like a problem. Even Arteta acknowledged that. "There are many areas that we need to improve. That's one, that's related sometimes to the timing or the situation, or really the position [of the opponent], where he's lined up and what space he's given you.

"Certainly it's far too many. It's true that the Villa game obviously he's putting those stats in a different perspective. I think the sample is quite short to analyse it, but you have a point there."

As for the Villa game, Mikel, yes, that's eight of your 35. Leeds is seven, though. Coventry five, Hull four. These are all well above the Premier League average. The chief culprit for this spate of infractions is certainly Havertz. His 15 offsides are not just seven more than any other player in the top flight; they are more than any Arsenal player committed in the entirety of last season's title campaign.

Again, this feels a little unprecedented. In the six seasons prior to this one, Havertz ranked 48th among forwards in the division for how frequently they were caught offside. The worst offenders, your Ashley Barneses, Darwin Nunezes and Cristiano Ronaldos, might get flagged once every 70 or 80 minutes. Havertz hovered around the 140 mark. This season it's not far off once per half.

Has he lost some burst? Gradient Sports' physical data would suggest he is moving about as swiftly this season as any other. A broader view is that this attack might have greater joy punishing high lines with more pacey options in it. For a player who makes so many runs off the ball, Madueke is caught offside relatively infrequently (though his was one of the four today). That is probably because he can give his man a yard in a way that Havertz or even Bukayo Saka, third in the league with seven offsides, can't quite.

Have defenses sussed Havertz's movement out? That doesn't seem entirely clear, not least given that Hull misjudged their line more than once, allowing Havertz in a one-on-one position where he should have done much better than cut the ball onto Mendy's trailing leg.

Arteta's explanation is simple. "It's all about timing," he said. "So there is a signal on the ball, and you need to time it around that. If that's a second too late or half a second too late, that's all."

Certainly Arsenal could release the ball a bit quicker. If there is a flaw in the game of Odegaard, whose nine passes to an offside teammate also lead the league, it is that he tends to want that one extra touch. That much was apparent in the win at Aston Villa, when the captain had the ideal chance to slip Havertz through in position to bend one in the far post. He took three touches when two would have sufficed, and it was all a moment too late.

Bruno Guimaraes (four such passes) is in a similar vein. And perhaps Arsenal as a club are a bit too much of that ilk. Does the specter of Alex Hleb and Samir Nasri still haunt this team? Arteta might have said as much, that the thing about Arsenal is they always try to walk it in.

"We need to find ways to be more efficient, sometimes even more pragmatic," he said. "Sometimes my feeling is that we are trying to score a perfect goal against these low blocks. We need to be much more chaotic than that."

You can see that in some of those offsides above, especially the smattering around the right flank that Arsenal like to make their creative hub. It's the attempted reverse balls, the quick one-twos and slide-rule passes to a teammate on the overlap. Offside No. 36 might well have been another of those, an overlapping run from Jurrien Timber where Madueke released the pass a beat too late and the Dutchman stopped rather than cede Hull a free kick.

Instead, Madueke proved the value of an alternative approach right throughout this match. Driving at his fullback time and time again, he manufactured positions where things might happen without having to worry about a give-and-go or timing his run correctly. In an age where so many opponents, including Hull, are more intent on gumming up their opposition than gritting and grinding, a bit of unpredictability from one of Arsenal's own players goes a long way. As for the offsides, of course that feels like a problem, a lot of possessions wasted by Arsenal players' own inability to get on the right beat. It has been. It does not mean it is going to be. Injuries mean that Havertz and Odegaard have rarely shared the pitch over the last few seasons. Get them and Saka together for weeks on end and the old rhythm will come back to them, and this should be nothing more than a weird, if intriguing, blip.

#1322. New CRISPR therapy is poised to gain first FDA approval to alter genes inside the body

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

The Cas9 protein (blue; artist’s illustration) together with RNA and DNA (orange). A new therapy uses the CRISPR–Cas9 gene-editing system to treat a rare genetic disorder called hereditary angioedema.Credit: Alfred Pasieka/SPL

A pioneering therapy that edits genes inside a recipient’s body continues to be effective four years after treatment, according to data released by its developer, Intellia Therapeutics.

The therapy, named lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z), was designed to treat one form of a genetic condition that can cause episodes of painful and potentially dangerous swelling in the throat and other parts of the body. Lonvo-z deploys the CRISPR–Cas9 gene-editing system to disable the gene that produces prekallikrein, a protein made in the liver that promotes blood-vessel leakage.

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Intellia, headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has applied for approval of lonvo-z by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is expected to issue a decision by 10 March. If approved, the therapy will become the world’s first CRISPR medicine to be delivered directly inside the body, or in vivo, John Leonard, Intellia’s chief executive, told investors on 12 November. Currently, the only CRISPR therapy approved by the FDA is performed on cells that have been removed from the body and are subsequently re-infused.

For people with the condition, a type of hereditary angioedema, the gene-editing approach could offer relief from a lifetime of juggling medications to prevent and treat swelling attacks, says Jonathan Bernstein, a hereditary-angioedema specialist at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio and an investigator on a lonvo-z trial. “It’s very reassuring,” he says of the four-year data. “That’s what you’re supposed to see.”

The only approved CRISPR therapy is Casgevy, a treatment for two genetic blood disorders, sickle-cell disease and β-thalassaemia. To create a dose of Casgevy, physicians first remove blood stem cells from the recipient, then send the cells off for gene editing before infusing them back into the recipient.

The therapy must be made anew for each person, adding time, cost and complexity. The recipient also has to undergo harsh chemotherapy treatment to make room for the edited cells.

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

In vivo gene-editing approaches aim to sidestep these concerns by editing genes directly in the body. Lonvo-z, for example, consists of fatty particles that encase mRNA encoding CRISPR–Cas9 components. The particles are infused into the blood and taken up by the liver, where prekallikrein is produced. The procedure takes one day.

In vivo gene editing can introduce other safety concerns, however. The therapy affords no opportunity to screen out cells with unwanted edits at other locations in the genome. Recipients might also have harmful immune responses to the treatment.

Last year, the FDA placed a clinical hold on two of Intellia’s in vivo trials for a different disorder. The agency did so after a participant with additional health conditions developed signs of liver damage and died after receiving a CRISPR treatment. The FDA lifted the hold this year after extra safety measures were added.

It all begins with Washington.

#1319. Gotham FC, Seattle Reign slam 'atrocious' pitch conditions after NWSL playoff clash

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

HARRISON, N.J. – Gotham FC head coach Juan Carlos Amoros criticized the field conditions at Sports Illustrated Stadium during the team's 1-0 win over the Seattle Reign on Sunday, a complaint that highlighted the infrastructure battles the league is grappling with during this season's playoffs.

The NWSL fined Gotham $10,000 in the build-up to Sunday's quarterfinal over the quality of the pitch, which appears to have been overworked in recent weeks. Gotham are a secondary tenant at the stadium, which is owned by New Jersey's Hudson County and is primarily the home of the Red Bull New York. The MLS team played their regular season finale on Saturday evening, less than 24 hours before the 12:30 p.m. local time kickoff for the NWSL match. The stadium also hosted a rugby doubleheader the previous week, the scars of which were easy to spot over the course of Sunday's game.

"I feel the obligation to almost apologize for the state of the pitch," Amoros said post-match. "I think at this level, in this kind of game, as a league, we should be having a better surface. Unfortunately, our football club did absolutely everything in their power to make sure that was the case. Unfortunately, it wasn't but luckily, it looks like nobody got hurt and the game was what it was."

Players on both teams complained of the playing conditions, including Gotham's Jaelin Howell, who worked her way back from an ankle issue in time for Sunday's match.

"Obviously it's pretty sandy out there and so a little unstable but I want to be able to give my all to the team and everything I got and so obviously can't think about that," Howell said. "The other team has to play on that, too, so we acknowledged it and we moved on and I think that our team managed it pretty well for the most part."

The Reign's Jess Fishlock, a member of Seattle's squad since the inaugural NWSL season in 2013 who played the final match of her career, was more harsh in her assessment of the field.

"We performed so well for this group of players to come against a team like that at home on this field, which is atrocious, just saying it out loud," she said.

Her comments were echoed by Reign coach Laura Harvey, who has worked in and around the league since its inception.

"Let's be real, there's no way a playoff game should be played on that shit," she told ESPN post-match. "I just can't believe they've allowed it. They knew it last week."

Amoros said the field conditions ultimately impacted Gotham's ability to perform on Sunday, the NWSL Shield winners stringing together a performance he described as "not the best football match that you will ever see."

"When you play on a pitch like that, you cannot be thinking of the next action or what you're gonna do once you get that ball," he said. "You need to be looking at the ball because he can bounce at any given time. Plus, it just changes the whole dynamic of the game and it changes the dynamic of how we play. We adapted certain things. We adapted certain things on the game plan. We had to be a bit more direct and certain situations but it definitely affected the way we played, yes."

Gotham will conclude play at Sports Illustrated Stadium next Sunday at 3 p.m. local time in the NWSL semifinals against the Kansas City Current. The Red Bulls, who missed the MLS Cup playoffs for a second consecutive season, will host another match the night before, this time a friendly against Club America during the men's international break.

The pitch was an understandable obstacle for both teams but Gotham's struggles did not end there. The reigning champions, who are favored to win the championship for the third time in four seasons after winning the Shield, were second-best against the lowest-seeded team in the postseason. They benefitted from a fourth minute own goal from Jordyn Bugg, forced by standout Jaedyn Shaw, but were unable to actually assert any sort of dominance as the game progressed.

An unfortunate own goal and Gotham take the early lead ‼️NWSL Playoffs presented by Google Pixel pic.twitter.com/4LwZdfgLpx

Gotham did not take a single shot on target over the course of the game, their six shots totaling just 0.17 expected goals. The Reign were not all that much better but momentum shifted their way in the second half, eventually racking up 11 shots and 0.54 expected goals. The visitors were stymied by Gotham defenders Tierna Davidson and Jess Carter, as well as 2024 goalkeeper of the year Ann-Katrin Berger.

"She literally does it on a consistent basis," Shaw said about Berger. "It's crazy the kind of saves that she makes and I feel like she makes a worldly save at least once a game and I mean I think it's hard enough getting through a back line but to get through Ann is a whole other task and I think we're all really grateful to have her back there. I know I am as an attacker and I think we all just have full trust in her ability and she's just such an integral part of our team and the way that we like to play as well. Even from the goal, she's such a big piece of the way that we play and our style."

AKB goes aerial to deny Mia Fishel a goal ✈️ pic.twitter.com/4lqMm623On

Gotham's attack, though, had no such excuses. Midfielder Rose Lavelle exited the match at halftime as the coaching staff manages her minutes after dealing with a knock in recent weeks, her exit diluting their attack. Forward Sam Kerr, meanwhile, failed to register a single shot and took just 23 touches over the course of 90 minutes in an absent performance during an inconsistent return to the NWSL. The Australia international has scored just four goals in 18 games since joining Gotham in July, despite the fact that she has racked up 9.67 expected goals along the way.

Amoros credited the Reign for their ability to lock out Gotham's defense.

"I think they did a good job trying to stop certain situations," he said. "I think that was the key. They did really well on the press. They were first and second in a lot of the duels and they obviously play short passes to then go diagonal, which obviously then is something difficult to defend and something that is a lot more doable than probably over a style of play. It's just different and we had issues with those situations to defend. At the same time, we defended them. I think that's the key."

Shaw, who attempted to spearhead a lifeless Gotham attack, described a disjointed performance that the team will hope not to replicate the following week.

"I think we just need to be cleaner on the ball," Shaw said. "Obviously, the surface doesn't really help but  just in general, I think we can be more comfortable on the ball, facing forward and just be clinical in our passes, which I think will help us get to the final third a little bit more with more quality chances on goal."

#1317. Switzerland 4-0 Scotland: Swiss stroll leaves serious question marks over Sebastien Pocognoli as Scots round off miserable campaign with defeat on captain Andrew Robertson's record-breaking night

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:06 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 18:08 EST, 16 November 2026

Despite re-establishing Scotland’s credentials as a credible football nation, by common consent, Steve Clarke’s time in charge of the side was up in the summer.

With qualification for a major tournament no longer satisfying the desires of the Tartan Army, a seven-year itch led to a parting of the ways.

In order to take that elusive step into a knock-out round, the theory went that employing a bolder coach who’d get more out of the players was all that was required. So much for that.

While few would dispute that a change at the helm was required, it was legitimate to question the wisdom in the SFA making one which was quite so radical. Those concerns have only been amplified by what’s been witnessed so far under Sebastien Pocognoli.

The Belgian is young, smart and intense. He won a title in Belgium with Union Saint-Gilloise and will have taken much from his brief, ill-fated spell at Monaco. He wants to play the kind of football supporters long to see.

But this Nations League campaign has been nothing short of dismal. Two wins from six matches, both of those coming against a poor North Macedonia side, and three nights to forget against the Swiss and Slovenia, is a lamentable record.

Andy Robertson endured a miserable night on the occasion of his record-breaking 103rd cap

Notwithstanding the fact that there were always likely to be teething problems, it’s fallen miles short of modest expectations.

Talk of it taking up to 18 months to all come up roses is all very well. But to believe that’s going to be the case, you need to see more green shoots at this point.

Having finished third in the section, Scotland are bound for pot three when the draw for Euro 2028 is made in Belfast next month.

Unless there’s a radical improvement come the qualifiers in March, it’s hard to see how Pocognoli’s side will get there by any means other than the back door.

This was another tough watch for the travelling supporters, one which will only lead to growing concerns about where all this is heading.

For half of a half, Scotland actually looked like they were getting somewhere under their new manager.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli faces some serious questions over a miserable campaign

From the minute Lewis Ferguson scored a horrible own goal, though, they became a rabble. Not nearly enough punch on the front foot. And far too easy to play through.

They shipped two goals inside five minutes early in the second half and looked like they’d have taken the final whistle there and then.

Individual mistakes from players are troubling Pocognoli in the same way they pockmarked the later days of Clarke’s reign.

Having witnessed Grant Hanley, Scott McKenna and Andy Robertson err in the World Cup, the Tartan Army had already seen Jack Hendry sent off against the Swiss at Hampden before Ferguson joined the growing list of sinners here.

Arriving midway through the first half, his unfathomable moment came when there wasn’t a red shirt in close proximity. It was a kick in the teeth for Pocognoli after a reasonable start.

While it would have been stretching matters to suggest that his team were vulnerable, Murat Yakin was without four of his big hitters in Manuel Akanji, Johan Manzambi, Dan Ndoye and Granit Xhaka.

There was a smattering of starters with five or six caps to their name. Two of the front three, Samuel Ballet and Winsley Boteli, were just 20.

Lewis Ferguson can't believe his misfortune after slicing the ball into his own net for the opener

It was a night when Scottish football history was made with Robertson winning his 103rd cap to finally rise above his great friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Pocognoli stuck by the back-three – Ryan Porteous, Luke Graham and Kieran Tierney – who acquitted themselves well against North Macedonia.

There was no great shock that the more defensive-minded Aaron Hickey replaced Ben Gannon-Doak on the right. Without a goal in 21 matches before a ball was kicked, Oli McBurnie’s selection ahead of Che Adams was intriguing.

The infuriating thing from Pocognoli’s perspective was that his side began with the right attitude.

Aside from an Isaac Schmidt shot which was fielded by Angus Gunn, they looked comfortable.

John McGinn’s pass into McBurnie saw the Hull forward flick the ball into space for Hickey to chase. Just when it looked like he might get a shot away, he was caught.

The positive early approach was typified by Porteous flying into a tackle 30 yards from the Swiss goal and winning the ball.

Winsley Boteli enjoys the moment after putting the stylish Swiss two goals ahead on the night

Had it not been for Hickey hesitating to pick out Scott McTominay’s run, the Napoli man would have been in on goal.

To put it mildly, the Swiss didn’t need an invitation to go down. The appropriately named Samuel Ballet was especially fond of the theatrics.

For a brief spell, Scotland had their opponents hemmed in. Pocognoli was miffed that two quick corners didn’t amount to anything.

Billy Gilmour probed and McTominay made key interceptions and sprayed passes. McGinn fired over.

At the midway point in the first half, there was much to admire. Then disaster struck.

The Swiss did well to advance down the right. Zachary Athekame simply launched a cross into the box and hoped for the best.

Aaron Hickey endured a painful injury blow and could now face another spell on the sidelines

With Ferguson running back towards goal and Porteous waiting to boot the ball to safety, there was no obvious danger.

For reasons only he could explain, the Bologna man stretched out a leg and watched on in horror as the ball sailed past Gunn. All that hard work undone in one desperate moment.

Hickey passed up a chance to immediately level when he headed Robertson’s cross wide. It was to be the Brentford man’s last meaningful involvement before he felt his hamstring tighten. Nathan Patterson replaced him.

A gift of a goal gave the Swiss a boost. Boteli launched himself at Alvyn Sanches’ cross. Gunn was untroubled.

Patterson did well to head Robertson’s deep cross back into the danger zone. McGinn’s header was straight into the arms of Yvon Mvogo.

For all Scotland were entitled to feel a little sore at being one down at the break, it could have been worse. The defence were completely static as Adrian Bajrami launched himself at a header. It was a good thing, from Gunn’s point of view, that the defender missed the target.

Alvyn Sanches drills home Switzerland's third goal in what was an entirely one-sided contest

Ferguson truly had a night to forget here. Within two minutes of the restart, he needlessly invited pressure when he launched a ball straight out of play.

Within seconds, with Porteous advanced, the Swiss broke down the left. Ballet fed Remo Freuler who returned the favour. Ballet rolled the ball towards goal from 12 yards with Boteli claiming the final touch. The visitors’ hopes of a VAR reprieve for offside were dashed.

And with that, the roof caved in. Patterson was dispossessed and Boteli worked the ball into the feet of Sanches. You could only admire the finish, but Scotland were an absolute mess in the build-up. It was threatening to get ugly.

With Tierney, Scotland’s best player on the night, lying on the deck, Ballet was only denied by Gunn. The Tartan Army looked at the clock and wished it was over.

With a minute remaining, a bad night got worse when Zeki Amdouni’s deflected shot beat Gunn.

Mercifully, this tortuous Nations League campaign can now be consigned to history. It’s been the most chastening experience for all concerned.

Right, where were we? Three weeks on from the fifth round of Premier League fixtures in which the champions Arsenal were beaten 3-0 by Brighton and todays’ visitors, Leeds United, who remain unbeaten, drew in a tepid goalless fixture with Crystal Palace, we finally get to the sixth. As worrying as the result was at the Amex, Arsenal still created a shedload of chances and last season they were the one club that battered Leeds in both games – first early in the season when they were playing four at the back and before Dominic Calvert-Lewin, a late signing, was fully fit, and then later after they had successfully switched to a “base formation” of three centre-backs and the tactical flexibility that allowed.

It was a 5-0 tanking in August and 4-0 in January, so to say Leeds travel to a ground at which they have never won more in hope than expectation would be as true as much as it is hackneyed. Adding to a sense of foreboding and thanks to Opta’s excellent Jonny Cooper, we also have to take into account the fact that Leeds, floodlight kings, have not won a Premier League match kicking off before 3pm since August 2022 and have not won a match in London since beating Brentford in May that year to save themselves from relegation. However, they do boast the division’s best defensive record – three goals conceded – and the No1 ranked goalkeeper in James Trafford who has a save percentage of 87. For all the sense of doom, though, Leeds have become a very good side and their spine – Trafford–Muharemovic–Ampadu–Calvert-Lewin marries steel and class.

Arsenall need no fanfare. Until the set-back in dear old Sussex by the sea, they had looked formidable most of the time and will have been champing at the bit to get back out there and prove it was an aberration. Mikel Arteta mentioned he has doubts about Declan Rice, Kai Havertz and Ezri Konsa but Ben White, Max Dowman and Chrsthian Mosquera are all available. For Leeds Joe Rodon is still out and Dan James was injured on international duty but Harry Wilson and Jean-Matteo Bahoya returned to training after knocks this week and Daniel Farke was relatively optimistic about their prospects.

#1315. How USMNT's Neil Pierre turned overseas loan into breakout season with Philadelphia Union

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

CHESTER, Pa. - Walking into Philadelphia Union training, there's one player who immediately sticks out due to towering over the rest of the team at center back: Neil Pierre. While a soft-spoken person in life, when you're 6-foot-7 on a soccer field, it's hard to miss him—even down to Chris Richards not believing it until he saw the Union defender in the United States Men's National Team camp. But height may also be the least interesting thing about Pierre's journey as he, like the Union, has taken MLS by storm since he returned from a loan spell in Denmark with Lyngby, where he helped the club gain promotion back to the Danish Superliga while getting a taste of what first-team soccer is like.

For an 19-year-old, just going to a new country is enough of an adjustment, and doing so while needing to break into a squad with ambition is quite a task, and Pierre did it while also learning a new position. Because of the club setup, Pierre actually played right back, and explaining the setup to CBS Sports, one of his co-managers, Andreas Bjelland, wanted to find out how he could get the talented young defender into the squad.

"He had the power, he had the drive, but he still needed the game smartness and the calmness of playing more senior minutes," Bjelland said. "And then he could get some extra minutes playing right back because we also had some really good center backs at that point playing really well. So it was a little bit of a mix of also getting him into play more and more."

This is a credit not only to Pierre's talent but also to his drive and versatility, as the Union man turned this into an excellent breakout where he scored four goals in 10 appearances while winning promotion and building confidence that he could do it as a soccer player along the way. Both the Union Academy and Pierre's own family helped set him up for success in a year that has become an absolute whirlwind. Following his success at Lyngby, alongside the Union falling to the bottom of the league, it was easy to question why Pierre wasn't with the team to start the season, but his time in Denmark was also formative. While it's easy to say that he should've been in Philadelphia from the start in hindsight, it was an important step for the Pierre that we see before us today.

"In the beginning, it was definitely a little nerve-wracking and definitely nervous," Pierre said, reflecting during Philadelphia Union training. "I think I can give all credit to them; they've kind of taken me in as like a part of the family immediately, so I felt like there was no stress there, and then that translated to on the pitch and they gave me the confidence to play how I was supposed to play. And then also off the field, I think, because we would go to team outings all the time and get dinner together, so it was like a family on and off the field."

Fast forward, and not only has Pierre been part of pulling the Union out of the bottom of the Eastern Conference, but he's also earned his first USMNT call-up and cap, and that was quickly followed by a return call for Concacaf Nations League play, where the USMNT will face Haiti twice during this international window, but if not for his family, soccer may not have happened. When Pierre was younger, basketball was the first sport that he connected with, but he credits his brother Nelson Pierre (who is currently on loan from the Vancouver Whitecaps to the HFX Wanderers of the Canadian Premier League) and his father for why he is where he is now.

"If it wasn't for them, I would be playing basketball right now. 100%," Pierre said. "But I think through them it was like I saw the love they had for the sport, and like how much passion they had, so I was like obviously I wanted to follow in my dad and brother's footsteps and be able to have that passion for something. So then I followed them into soccer and it's been since ever since it's been like this."

Considering his play for the Union this season, plenty are happy that Pierre made the decision to stick with soccer, but while his frame and closing speed do come with advantages, they also comes with things that he has to watch out for on the field, especially when defending against smaller players. Not only are they at times more agile than Pierre, but challenges that he makes can look worse too, and these are things that gaining more in-game experience has helped him prepare for, dealing with them and excelling.

He also has the benefit of playing not only for a coach that he knows from the Union youth ranks, but also for one who was a defender during his own professional career. In fact, Pierre has always had a defensive-minded head coach, even with the USMNT in Mauricio Pochettino, and that's something else that has been a benefit while he's getting his feet in the game.

"Obviously, being young, playing with older players [my coaches have] pulled me aside, either showing me film or what they feel like they've seen, and it's obviously different hearing it from a coach that's played in your position and done it at the highest level," Pierre said. "Same with the national team with Poch, I think hearing stuff like that, it's like these guys have done it at a pro level for a long time, so they know what they're talking about."

Add that to his natural skills, and you get a young defender that the Union can anchor the squad around. Before even getting into his goals, his closing speed and positioning are able to anchor a defense that has allowed the third-fewest goals in MLS since the World Cup, with only 21. They may not have risen to first in the Eastern Conference, but when the squad only had seven points prior to the World Cup and has picked up 40 after it so far, the impact that Pierre and the rest of the squad have had to push their way into the playoffs has been quite remarkable. You can also see why Lyngby wanted to keep him for their season in the Danish top flight, but when the Union had a chance at a starting spot, it was hard to allow Pierre to go back on loan when he could help the first team.

"We can be super aggressive because Neil is comfortable in one-on-one situations. If it's a direct ball, he wins; he eats all of these. If it's open space that he has to defend, physically, he can deal with that, and he's also a good defender," Philly's interim coach, Ryan Richter, said about how Pierre's play impacts his squad. "The way he puts out so many fires allows us to be aggressive higher up the field, because we know when they play the ball long that we have someone who cleans this up almost every time."

Defenders usually peak later than attackers in soccer, so it's impressive that Pierre is catching on so quickly, but given his path of getting into first-team soccer and also being with the coach who he came up through the academy with, it's a good spot for Pierre to succeed and grow before his next step likely takes him back to Europe.

"I think as a person, he's much more mature and much more focused than I would say at the point he was at a year ago, when I was coaching him with the second team. I'm really proud of him, the way that he's been able to put focus on the day-to-day and the game-to-game," Richter said. "Because I think of a lot of things, positive and negative, that happened to him this year. Having a great experience in Denmark, but it didn't start out perfect, and he earned his way in. When he came back here, he earned the starting spot. A couple months later called for the national team for his first caps to the national team. Comes back and is able to right away again put his full attention back in with the team and play a couple of good games after that. Um, so overall, his maturity in dealing with the things that are going on around him, I think, has been really impressive."

Pierre credits his family and the team for helping him stay grounded through what has been an absolute whirlwind year. Next up is a trip to USMNT camp before helping anchor the defense for the club as they face the New England Revolution in the first round of the MLS Cup playoffs. Plenty for a young player to juggle, but after the year Pierre has had, this will feel more normal than what he has already accomplished.

#1313. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

When asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”

3 - Manchester United have failed to win any of their last three Premier League games against sides that have received a red card (D1 L2). Disadvantage? https://t.co/DuSpvymZfu

The Tottenham boss told Sky Sports: “I think we played very well against a great team. We had many chances to score in the first half. Three or four. The second half is normal to suffer against this quality. I am very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character.

We have to react in all ways we can. It is a bad way, it is not the right way. I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character.

“We win the game if we play as a team. We didn’t win this game playing as a team. Every game like today, we will win many games.”

When asked about Solanke, he replied: “He is a good player for Tottenham. There for not too many strikers better than Solanke. “We have to believe in ourselves and this football way. If we believe, improve and play as a team, we will score many goals and win many games. If we don’t play as a team, it is impossible.”

#1310. Daily briefing: Are one-person firms the future of biotech?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) and lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) across Brazil have traces of microplastics circulating in their blood — even if they live more than 60 kilometres away from human infrastructure. Researchers found that these animals carry roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood on average — similar to the levels of plastics found in humans — with the highest levels found in those that lived closest to urban areas and waste-management facilities. The findings are an important step to better understand how these particles impact wildlife, says geochemist Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou.

Artificial-intelligence giant Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2, an upgrade to their AI tool that predicts the molecular effects of ‘non-coding’ DNA sequences. The tool, announced on 11 November, has already impressed researchers. Its underlying AI model was trained on gene activity and other measurements made in more than 100 million individual cells, across 68 tissues. But the tool can also make predictions when fed data from cell types that it wasn’t trained on, which could help researchers more quickly identify variants underlying disease, says DeepMind scientist Adam Gayoso.

An approach that measures waist circumference and focuses on excess body fat could be a more accurate way to diagnose obesity — and identify people with related health risks — than body mass index (BMI). In an analysis of data from more than 800,000 people, researchers found that using BMI to diagnose obesity failed to identify a considerable proportion of people with elevated health risks caused by excess body fat. The new framework classified an extra 5–9% of people as having obesity, who would have been labelled only as overweight with the BMI-based approach.

Bioengineered bacteria that ‘fix’ nitrogen into a useful form for plants could replace up to half of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers, slashing the greenhouse-gas emissions associated with these chemicals, researchers suggest. Bacteria can deliver nitrogen to roots more efficiently than synthetic fertilizers, and scientists are engineering them to feed nitrogen to crop plants that don’t have natural microbial partners, such as maize and wheat. Gene-edited biofertilizers have already been used in the United States, but a slew of advances are needed to demonstrate higher levels of nitrogen fixation.

In July, artificial-intelligence titan Anthropic acquired a biotechnology company that developed two promising drug leads with just one full-time human employee and an AI assistant. The mini-firm benefited from the help of several part-time consultants and external research organizations to craft its products — two early-stage antibodies designed to treat a rare form of muscular dystrophy — and many more researchers will be required to take the drugs forward. But the acquisition has sparked discussion about whether one-person, AI-enabled biotech is the drug-discovery business model of the future.

With the rise of multidisciplinary science and artificial intelligence, biologists are “poised to at last understand the complexity of life”, writes epigeneticist Edith Heard, chief executive of the Francis Crick Institute, London. But people are what will unlock these discoveries, not technology alone. “Funders, institutions and scientific leaders must embrace new technologies while protecting the conditions in which discovery thrives: curiosity, collaboration and, above all, the freedom and support to follow unexpected observations to see where they lead,” Heard writes.

“Environmental change is altering the conditions in which brains develop and minds are sustained”, says a new report from a commission convened by Nature Mental Health. For example, heat, air and noise pollution and loss of green space have been linked with depression, anxiety and cognitive decline — with poorer people, children and older people among those most exposed. The Earth–Brain–Health Commission offers a new framework for uniting neuroscience, psychiatry, public health and environmental science around shared challenges and solutions.

Nature Mental Health editorial | 6 min read

Get the gist in the accompanying policy brief (9 min read)

Reference: Nature Mental Health Earth–Brain–Health Commission report

The lawless simulated world of blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto (GTA) — which is just about to release its sixth iteration — offers researchers an intricately crafted testbed for road-safety experiments, says computer scientist Julius Schöning. (BBC | 7 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03684-x

Today I’m adding M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything to my reading list. The post-apocalyptic novel was announced as the winner of this year’s Booker prize on 9 November — the first “bona fide” science-fiction novel to win the award, says Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation.

Let me know what other science-fiction books I should add to the pile, along with your feedback on this newsletter, at briefing@nature.com.

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing

#1307. Gotham FC move NWSL semifinal against Kansas City Current to Icahn Stadium over pitch quality concerns

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Gotham FC will play Sunday's NWSL semifinal against the Kansas City Current at Icahn Stadium over concerns about the quality of the pitch at Sports Illustrated Stadium, which was described as "atrocious" during the team's quarterfinal win over the Seattle Reign.

The NWSL Shield winners announced the venue shift on Monday, less than a week before the semifinal. Icahn Stadium is a smaller venue on Manhattan's Randall's Island that seats 5,000 and has been sparingly used by Gotham, who have played the vast majority of their home games at Sports Illustrated Stadium in Harrison, N.J. since 2021. Sports Illustrated Stadium seats 25,000 and welcomed nearly 13,000 for Sunday's 1-0 win over the Reign.

The quarterfinal match, though, was marred by complaints about the playing surface from both teams. Reign head coach Laura Harvey described the field as "shit" in a post-match interview with ESPN, while captain Jess Fishlock called it "atrocious." Gotham head coach Juan Carlos Amoros also apologized for the quality of the surface after the NWSL fined the club $10,000 in the build-up to the quarterfinal match.

"We as a team worked extremely hard to earn a home playoff berth," captain Tierna Davidson said in a statement on Monday. "What we got was a field that is not the standard this club, this league, or our fans deserve. The quality of the game is not up for debate, so we've made the difficult decision to move to Icahn Stadium on Sunday. A smaller stadium means many of you will not be there, and that is the hardest part of this decision. You have turned every ground where we have played into home, and that does not change on Sunday. We have never needed a perfect setting to make a place ours. Bring everything you have on Sunday, and we will leave it all on the field."

The pitch at Sports Illustrated Stadium appeared to show the wear and tear from recent events, not least of which was Gotham's regular season slate. Gotham are the secondary tenants at the venue, which is owned by New Jersey's Hudson County but counts MLS' Red Bull New York as the primary tenants and operators of the facility. The stadium was also the site of a rugby doubleheader the weekend before Gotham's quarterfinal against the Reign, which led Gotham midfielder Jaelin Howell to describe the surface as "sandy" and "unstable."

The Red Bulls will still play a friendly on Saturday at Sports Illustrated Stadium against Club America. The friendly will take place during the men's international break, so several first-team players will miss the match, which will serve as the final game of their season since they missed out on the MLS Cup playoffs for a second season in a row.

"We wish Gotham FC the best of luck in their semifinal at Icahn Stadium," Red Bull New York told CBS Sports in a statement. "We look forward to our match on Saturday at Sports Illustrated Stadium."

Gotham have staged two games at Icahn Stadium in the last year and change – a Concacaf W Champions Cup group stage match in 2025 and their 3-2 win over the Reign in July. There is the perception of convenience for the club's fans based in the city of New York, who would otherwise have to trek to New Jersey to attend a game. As far as public transportation goes, though, Icahn Stadium is only accessible via the M35 bus; a footbridge connecting Randall's Island to 125th Street is also an option, as is driving to the stadium.

"It's nice for folks who live in New York to have a somewhat closer venue," Jen Muller, a longtime member of the official Gotham supporters group Cloud 9, told CBS Sports last year. "I know it's not ideal for a lot of them, too, because there's one bus that comes here, but you adapt."

The pitch at Icahn Stadium, which has also hosted New York City FC II matches this year, is not expected to be an issue and was not during the Concacaf match in 2025.

"I don't really want to talk too much about it, but the Sports Illustrated Stadium has traditionally been the best pitch in the league," Amoros said at the time, "and the last couple of games, it's definitely been far away from that, so this pitch here is outstanding."

Gotham's move to Icahn comes despite the fact that they avoided a scheduling conflict with Sunday's results. The NWSL's broadcast slots for this year's semifinals were Saturday at 12 p.m. ET on CBS and Paramount+ and Sunday at 3 p.m. ET on ABC; the Washington Spirit will host the Utah Royals on Saturday, while Gotham will take on the Current on Sunday.

For Gotham, the Sunday time slot was the preferred option because of a pre-existing scheduling conflict with the Red Bulls' Saturday friendly against Club America. They had to wait out the result of the Spirit's quarterfinal with the Portland Thorns, though, since the Thorns would have been unable to host a semifinal at 9 a.m. local time. Gotham seemed destined to return to Sports Illustrated Stadium once they avoided the scheduling conflict but the quality of the pitch caused new concerns.

The Spirit, meanwhile, avoided a scheduling conflict of their own. They were originally set to host the Royals at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Md., home of the NFL's Washington Commanders, because their usual venue of Audi Field was instead hosting Secretaries' Cup, a Division III college football game between the United States Merchant Marine Academy and the United States Coast Guard Academy. The college football game has since been pushed to a later slot that day, Spirit CEO Kim Stone crediting Audi Field owners D.C. United and sponsor Lafayette Federal Credit Union for underwriting "the additional costs necessary to bring this semifinal match home."

The issues stem from the fact that many NWSL teams are secondary tenants in their home stadiums, the Spirit included – MLS' D.C. United own and operate Audi Field. Some, like the Royals and the Orlando Pride, benefit from sharing ownership groups with MLS clubs, while the Current own and operate CPKC Stadium. The rest often rent the local MLS team's stadium, Gotham and the Spirit included, but it creates other unique conflicts for teams with more control over their venues. The Current's quarterfinal against Angel City on Saturday, for example, kicked off at 11 a.m. local time in order to fit the broadcast slot on CBS.

#1306. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Erling Haaland gives Manchester City the lead against Liverpool 🎯 https://t.co/cELo5y60Fk

In fact, Liverpool’s best performers were the young attackers Victor Muñoz and, making his first league start as a makeshift centre-forward, Lewis Koumas, who is just 21. Against that, City unleashed a battery of forward talent.

"Koumas & Munoz were better than the two £100million players!" Jamie Carragher is still disappointed with what he's seeing from Florian Wirtz in a Liverpool shirt 😬🔴 https://t.co/jJwOZbPJ4b

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

With the football world still making sense of the news, Tony Pulis admits to feeling “cheated”. His Stoke City side were defeated by Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final, during the 2009-23 period.

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

It also discloses that image rights had been inflated and key witnesses had lied.

Ferran Soriano, chief executive of City Football Group, appears helpless when questioned about the verdict’s findings at the European Football Clubs’ general assembly in Copenhagen by Sky News.

With City on the ropes, Pep Guardiola releases a statement in support of his former club, assuring supporters that “we will get through this together”.

The Prime Minister says that he would be “really concerned” to lose City’s owners, but after significant backlash, No 10 moves to clarify his reaction saying that “if wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences”.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

The UAE then warns Andy Burnham that it will pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK in retaliation for the guilty verdict against City.

City argue that their sponsorship deals were part-funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owners, in their appeal, which claims bank statements and witness accounts provide “irrefutable evidence” to support their case.
